common_name: Windy City Dwarf Fothergilla (Extra-Cold-Hardy Compact Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Windy City tolerates colder winters than most dwarf fothergilla cultivars, making it a good choice for gardens at the cold edge of the species' range.

directions: Windy City is a Chicago-area seedling selection of the dwarf witch alder valued for tolerating colder winters than most Fothergilla gardenii cultivars, reliably surviving into USDA zone 4. In spring it carries the same honey-scented, bottlebrush-shaped white flower spikes typical of the species, opening on bare stems before the leaves fully expand. Its blue-green summer foliage turns a strong red in autumn, often outperforming other gardenii selections for fall color intensity. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where its compact two- to three-foot mound fits neatly into a foundation planting or woodland-edge border.

common_name: Huntsman Large Fothergilla (Slow-Growing Monticola Group Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Huntsman is slow-growing, often taking five to ten years to reach mature size, so site it where you can wait out its gradual fill-in.

directions: Huntsman belongs to the Monticola Group of Fothergilla major, a race of the species selected for smaller, more compact growth than typical seedling-grown plants. It is a slow grower, often taking five to ten years to reach its mature rounded shape, so gardeners should expect a gradual rather than quick fill-in. Thick, glossy, dark green leaves with softly downy undersides give way to warm orange and red fall tones, following spikes of white, upright flowers that open on bare wood in late spring before the foliage emerges. Plant in full sun to partial shade in humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil, and expect only light pruning needs given its naturally tidy habit.

common_name: Arkansas Beauty Large Fothergilla (Compact Ozark-Origin Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Arkansas Beauty tolerates dry spells better than typical seedling-grown Fothergilla major once its roots are established.

directions: Arkansas Beauty was discovered as a naturally more compact, less pubescent-leaved population of Fothergilla major growing in a disjunct Ozark Mountain valley of Searcy County, Arkansas, well outside the species' usual Appalachian and Piedmont range. It forms a mounded shrub bearing the same fragrant, white, bottlebrush-shaped spring flower spikes as the species, followed by fall foliage that mixes red, orange, and yellow, though typically less intensely colored than selections like Mount Airy. Once established it shows notably better drought tolerance than typical seedling-grown Fothergilla major, a useful trait for gardeners in hotter, drier summer climates. Grow in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

common_name: Black Mountain Large Fothergilla (Compact Upright Dark-Leaved Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Black Mountain stays noticeably narrower and more upright than typical seedling-grown Fothergilla major, suiting tighter planting spaces.

directions: Black Mountain is a more upright and compact-growing selection of Fothergilla major, staying noticeably tighter and narrower than typical seedling-grown plants of the species. Its small, leathery, dark green leaves give the shrub a denser, more refined texture through the growing season than looser-habited cultivars. Like other Fothergilla major forms it produces fragrant white bottlebrush flower spikes on bare stems in mid-spring, though its fall color is generally considered subdued compared with showier selections such as Mount Airy. Grow in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where its compact upright form suits a foundation planting or narrow border space.

common_name: Feist Red Large Fothergilla (Large Stout-Branched Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Feist Red grows into a large, sturdy-branched shrub, so allow more room than compact selections like Huntsman or Black Mountain.

directions: Feist Red is a large-growing selection of Fothergilla major, developing an oval, rounded outline on notably stout, sturdy branching that holds up well without staking or support. It produces the species' typical fragrant, upright, white bottlebrush flower spikes on bare stems in mid- to late spring, and its cultivar name points to the red-toned fall foliage display it was selected to showcase. Because it grows larger than compact selections like Black Mountain or Huntsman, it needs more room and works best as a background shrub or specimen rather than a tight foundation planting. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

common_name: Russell Montgomery American Beautyberry (White-Fruited Gulf Coast Native Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Russell Montgomery is a white-fruited selection prized in Gulf Coast and Southeastern gardens for its fall fruit display and wildlife value.

directions: Russell Montgomery is a white-fruited selection of American beautyberry, distinct from the more commonly offered 'Alba' and 'Lactea' selections but sharing their departure from the species' typical magenta-purple fall fruit. Small, pale lavender-pink flowers cluster tightly in the leaf axils along arching stems in summer, followed by dense whorls of ivory-white berries that ripen in fall and often persist after the leaves drop. Like the species, it forms a loose, rounded, multi-stemmed shrub valued across the Gulf Coast and greater Southeast for its wildlife value, since songbirds readily strip the fruit clusters through fall and winter. Grow in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune hard in late winter since flowers and fruit form on the current season's new growth.
